analysis.one_liner: Extends Medicare coverage to every American, paying for it with new payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: Kennedy's Medicare for All bill, with no cosponsors, went to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a new Medicare program covering every U.S. citizen and legal resident who isn't already on Medicare, with benefits at least as good as what Members of Congress get. It would phase in coverage over about a decade — starting with children and people over 55, then expanding until everyone is covered by year 11. People could keep choosing their own doctor, or join a private plan as long as it offers benefits at least as good as federal employees get. It would be paid for with a 1.7% payroll tax on workers and a 7% payroll tax on employers. Kennedy introduced it in January 2006 with no cosponsors; it went to the Senate Finance Committee and never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans and people priced out of coverage — the bill would eventually guarantee Medicare-level coverage to all citizens and legal residents, with reduced cost-sharing for low-income people, mental health parity, and drug coverage as good as the federal employee plan.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare for All program covering every U.S. citizen and lawfully present resident not already on Medicare, phased in over roughly a decade — first children and people over 55, then expanding to everyone by year 11.

Requires benefits at least as comprehensive as Medicare's, including prescription drug coverage as good as the federal employee Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan, mental health parity, and reduced cost-sharing for low-income people.

Guarantees people can choose their own doctor, and lets them join private plans only if those plans offer benefits at least as good as what Members of Congress receive under the federal employee program.
Prevents states from cutting Medicaid eligibility or benefits below 2006 levels, so the new program supplements rather than replaces existing safety-net coverage.
Prohibits insurers from paying financial rebates to enrollees in the new program's private plans, and requires those plans to meet federal solvency, fraud, and auditing standards.

analysis.who_pays: Workers pay a new 1.7% tax on wages, employers pay a new 7% tax on wages, and self-employed people pay a combined tax on their income. Private health insurers would face strict new contract requirements and could no longer pay rebates to enrollees.

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax structure takes no account of family size or other personal circumstances, so it functions as a flat tax on wages regardless of a household's total income or need.
Coverage phases in over about a decade, so many uninsured adults in their 30s and 40s would wait years for coverage.
The bill's tax is levied on wages, which could pressure employers to shift compensation away from wages, and it does not address health care costs driven by prices rather than insurance coverage.
It would not cover undocumented immigrants, so a significant uninsured population would remain outside the program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered universal coverage — arguably the most comprehensive health care expansion ever proposed in this period — but paid for it with an unusually blunt payroll tax rather than a progressive income tax. The long phase-in meant adults in middle age would wait up to a decade for coverage. Whether the coverage gains outweighed the tax structure and the wait was the core political debate; the bill never advanced far enough for Congress to weigh that trade-off in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its Finance Committee in January 2006; the committee never acted on it, and Congress ended without the bill receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Kennedy introduced the bill on January 31, 2006 and the Senate immediately referred it to the Finance Committee, which handles health care financing.
No cosponsors signed on, so the bill had no co-sponsorship base to build support within the Senate.
The Finance Committee took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and employers gained from the bill dying: they avoided new payroll taxes and avoided being bound into a program where private plans had to match federal-employee benefit levels with no rebates allowed. The uninsured gained nothing — they remained without coverage.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: None
for.what_they_did: No other senators signed on as cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, letting it sit until Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair, did not bring the bill up for committee action during 2006.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by the most prominent Democratic senator on health care and attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so there was no bipartisan support to force committee action.

industries.note: The bill lets private plans participate as contractors but only on strict terms — benefits as good as Members of Congress get, no rebates to enrollees, and federal oversight of solvency and fraud. Insurers would avoid the new program's payroll taxes only by avoiding wage-based employment.
A new 7% payroll tax on wages, which employers pay directly, would raise labor costs for most businesses.
A new 1.7% wage tax (and a combined tax on self-employment income) in exchange for guaranteed coverage that many would receive only after a multi-year phase-in.
